<<< fixed section: recovery scams >>>
== Watch out for recovery scams (DRAFT, not yet approved) ==
After a loss, people are often contacted by someone who says they can get the money back: a "recovery service", a "blockchain investigator", someone claiming to be a lawyer, or someone claiming to be from a government agency. Many of these are a second scam aimed at the same victim.

  - No one can reverse a confirmed blockchain transaction. Funds come back only when an exchange or issuer freezes them and a court or law enforcement acts.
  - Law enforcement does not charge victims a fee, and does not ask for payment in crypto, gift cards or wire transfers.
  - Tokens or messages sent to an address that advertise "unfreezing" or recovery are the same scheme. Do not contact the names, handles or websites in them.
  - If a platform says you must pay a fee or a tax before you can withdraw your money, that request is part of the scam. Do not send more money: paying does not release anything.
  - Be wary of anyone who contacts you first, asks for an upfront fee, asks for your wallet's recovery phrase or private key, or asks you to install remote-access software.
  - TraceAWallet will never contact you to offer recovery, and never asks for payment.

If someone offers recovery, report that contact at ic3.gov as well.
<<< end of fixed section >>>

<<< fixed section: IC3 checklist >>>
== Reporting what happened (DRAFT, not yet approved) ==
Report promptly. How quickly a report is made affects whether funds can still be frozen before they move on.

  [ ] First, tell the exchange or wallet provider you sent from. Ask them to flag the transfer and record your report.
  [ ] File with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) at ic3.gov.
  [ ] In the US, also report to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
  [ ] Outside the US, report to your national police or fraud reporting centre, and at econsumer.gov, which consumer protection agencies in many countries use for cross-border scams.

Gather these for the report:
  [ ] Each payment you made: the date, the amount, the asset (for example USDT on Tron) and the transaction hash
  [ ] The address you sent from, and the address you sent to (this report's address: 0xfa0a50dc366e2f0a5381e4d4b5fede589ab633a9 on Ethereum)
  [ ] The exchange or wallet app you sent from, and your account details there
  [ ] The names, usernames, phone numbers, email addresses and websites the other party used
  [ ] Messages, screenshots and any documents they sent you
  [ ] The platform or app you were told to use, with its web address

Keep the complaint ID IC3 gives you, and give it to the exchange you sent from.
<<< end of fixed section >>>
